content: PATH collaborated with 28 social media influencers from the LGBTQI+ community to promote awareness and engagement. These influencers were supported to create two posts per week from December 2022 to February 2023. The posts included a variety of content such as photos with messages, animated and personal videos, quizzes, and polls. Over the course of the campaign, 374 posts were created, which collectively garnered 830,900 views and engaged 54,000 individuals. Additionally, 7,644 people clicked on links to explore the virtual platform, 321 individuals registered, and 112 ordered test kits. Further demand generation through dating platforms and other social media channels resulted in an additional 346 test kit orders. The influencer marketing strategy demonstrated a higher uptake of services within a short timeframe compared to previous approaches. Users of the platform also interacted with influencers, providing valuable insights into testing behaviors and feedback on packaging and delivery mechanisms. This feedback was used to refine campaign messaging. Effective demand generation through social media requires time, strategic focus, and meaningful engagement with the target audience. However, converting this demand into actual uptake of HIV self-testing (HIVST) services necessitates additional support and a deeper understanding of the testing needs and preferences of the virtual population. The World Health Organization (WHO) has updated its recommendations regarding pre-test counseling for HIV testing. With the integration of HIV testing into routine healthcare, the use of rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs), and the availability of effective prevention and treatment options, individualized pre-test counseling is no longer deemed necessary. Instead, concise pre-test information should be provided, addressing general information, answering client questions, and offering the option to decline testing. Lengthy pre-test counseling has been shown to have minimal impact on risk behaviors or HIV knowledge and may deter testing, particularly among populations requiring frequent retesting. Programs may deliver pre-test information through individual or group sessions, as well as via media such as posters, brochures, websites, or short videos in waiting areas. When pre-test information is required, concise messaging should include the benefits of HIV testing, the implications of positive or negative results, the importance of treatment as prevention (e.g., Undetectable = Untransmittable or U=U), available services for those who test positive, and the confidentiality of test results. Clients should also be informed of their right to refuse testing without affecting their access to other medical services. Post-test services should be tailored to the specific needs of individuals based on their test results. For those testing HIV-positive, counseling should focus on promoting adherence to antiretroviral therapy (ART) to achieve viral suppression, emphasizing the prevention benefits of ART (U=U), and offering network-based testing services for partners and other at-risk individuals. Rapid linkage to ART initiation is critical, and WHO recommends co-located and well-coordinated ART services, peer support, and provider-assisted partner services to facilitate this process. Lengthy post-test counseling is generally unnecessary for those at low risk, as it may deter future testing. Instead, concise and client-centered messaging should be provided, with a focus on prevention options for those at substantial risk. HIV testing services (HTS) are incomplete without effective linkage to appropriate prevention, treatment, and care services. This linkage is essential for individuals testing positive, those retesting positive, and those testing negative. Diagnosing individuals with HIV and facilitating early ART initiation is crucial for improving health outcomes and reducing transmission. HTS also provides an opportunity to re-engage individuals who have previously tested positive but are not on treatment or have discontinued ART. Post-test services should include clear and concise messaging tailored to the client’s needs, up-to-date information on U=U, and referrals for rapid ART initiation or prevention services. For those testing HIV-positive, counseling should address the need for retesting to confirm results, the chronic but manageable nature of HIV, and the benefits of immediate ART initiation. Clients should also be supported in addressing barriers to starting ART and provided with follow-up arrangements if needed. For individuals testing HIV-negative, providers should assess their risk and offer appropriate prevention options such as PrEP or PEP. Innovative tools, such as the B-OK bead bottles, have been developed to simplify complex concepts during counseling sessions. These bottles use beads to visually represent the progression of HIV and the impact of ART, helping clients understand the importance of adherence and viral suppression. This tool has been successfully implemented in multiple countries, improving client-provider communication and increasing motivation for linkage to care and adherence to treatment. In summary, effective HIV testing services require tailored preand post-test messaging, rapid linkage to care, and the integration of prevention and treatment services. Programs must address the unique needs of individuals based on their test results and provide clear, concise, and client-centered communication to support engagement in care and prevention.
